title: How much does medical animation cost? What drives the price
overview: How much does medical animation cost? The factors that drive the price of medical device and mechanism of action animation, from length and 3D detail to medical review.
author: Made Clear
body:
How much does medical animation cost? It's one of the first questions medtech teams ask, and the honest answer is that it depends on a handful of choices you make at the start. Two animations of the same length can differ widely in cost because one is a simple 2D explainer and the other is a scientifically detailed 3D mechanism of action film reviewed by a medical team in several markets.

Rather than quote numbers that won't fit your project, this guide explains what actually drives the price, so you can scope a medical animation that does the job without paying for things you don't need.

1. Length and complexity

Every second of finished animation has to be designed, built, animated and rendered. Longer films cost more, but complexity matters just as much: a single device shown in one environment is far simpler than a procedure that moves through several anatomical views, with blood flow, tissue and multiple instruments. A focused 60 to 90 second film on one idea is often more effective, and better value, than a long film that tries to explain everything.

2. 2D, 3D or a mix

2D motion graphics suit data, processes and simple diagrams. 3D medical animation is needed when the audience must understand anatomy, depth and how a device behaves inside the body. 3D takes more modelling, lighting and rendering, so it costs more. Many projects mix the two: 3D for the mechanism, 2D for the data around it.

3. Scientific accuracy and medical review

A medical device animation has to be right. Anatomy, scale, device behaviour and the sequence of a procedure all need checking by people who understand them. That means research at the start and clinical review during production. For Philips ICE in the Heart, we produced a medical-grade animation showing the end-to-end use of the VeriSight Pro ICE catheter in the LAAO procedure, detailed enough for physicians, radiographers and cath lab staff to learn from.

4. Mechanism of action animation

A mechanism of action animation explains how a therapy works at a level no camera can reach: how a stent expands, how energy travels through tissue, how a drug binds. These are usually the most detailed and most reviewed parts of a project, because they carry the core scientific claim. On The Curious Case of Coronary Calcium, the brief was to make the counterintuitive physics of intravascular lithotripsy felt, not just explained, combining live action with CGI inside a VR experience.

5. Reusing assets

3D models of a device and the anatomy around it take time to build, but once built they can be reused. A model made for a launch film can power training content, congress loops, sales tools, social clips and VR. Planning for reuse from the start lowers the cost of every piece that follows.

6. Revisions and approvals

Medical content usually passes through medical, legal and regulatory (MLR) review, sometimes in several countries. Each round of changes takes time, and late changes to a rendered 3D sequence are expensive. The best way to control cost is to agree the script and storyboard thoroughly before animation starts, with the reviewers involved early.

7. Voiceover, languages and versions

Professional voiceover, music and sound design add polish. Every additional language adds translation, voice recording, on-screen text changes and another review. For Medtronic's HTN:RDN programme, content was localised in six languages. Plan versions up front so the animation is built to make them easy, for example by keeping text separate from the picture.

8. Combining animation with live action

Sometimes the most convincing approach mixes animation with real footage. For Big Discrepancies, Big Solutions, we worked with model makers and stop-motion animators to build life-sized and oversized transparent artery models, then filmed iVascular's Angiolite stent expanding inside them. Physical models and stop-motion have their own costs, but they can prove a point that CGI alone might not.

How to get an accurate quote

To scope a medical animation properly, a good 3D medical animation company will ask:

  • Who is the audience, and what should they understand or do afterwards?
  • Where will it be shown: congress screens, field sales, education platforms, social?
  • How long should it be, and what has to be shown in 3D?
  • What existing assets, such as CAD files or previous models, can be used?
  • Who will review it, and how many rounds should you allow?
  • Which languages and versions do you need?

Clear answers to these questions make the quote accurate and the project smoother. If you'd like to talk through a medical animation, see our animation and illustration work or get in touch.
